 The United States Department of Justice on Monday said it has reached a settlement with the University of North Carolina that will close up to 18 civil rights investigations into the university.
 According to the Justice Department, its Office for Civil Rights entered a voluntary, university-wide agreement with UNC to end what it called antisemitism and discrimination. Kimberly Richey, assistant secretary of the Department of Education's Office for Civil Rights, said the settlement is an important step in upholding civil rights and "restoring faith in the American people's confidence in higher education."
 Other WRAL Top Stories
 “The Trump Administration is holding schools accountable for antisemitism at American universities and ensuring that institutions, which have no problem accessing generous taxpayer support, follow all federal laws and ensure safe learning environments," Richey said.
 Because the university settled, the Justice Department said it closed 18 active investigations into UNC, and the Civil Rights Division would end its 18-month compliance review. 
 In a statement, UNC said the agreement ensures Carolina’s eligibility to compete for federal grants, contracts and awards, including funding that supports the university’s research mission. UNC said the settlement neither admitted wrongdoing or liability nor made a monetary settlement payment.
 “This announcement reinforces our commitment to the fair and equal treatment of everyone at Carolina,” said Chancellor Lee H. Roberts. “For at least a decade, through different presidential administrations, U.S. universities have faced heightened public scrutiny across a range of issues. We’re proud to resolve those issues at Carolina in a way that protects our mission and affirms the civil rights of everyone in our community.”  
 What are the key takeaways of the settlement?
 As part of the settlement, the Justice Department said the school will hire a Title VI coordinator, who will help the university enforce, assess, and discipline antisemitism claims, as well as provide system-wide antisemitism training for UNC students and staff and a ban on facemasks that hide someone's identity. 
 It is unclear who would define what is or isn't antisemitic, particularly when it comes to disciplining the conduct of student groups, or how the university would enforce the mask ban and how broad or narrow it would be.
 The university said the settlement recognizes the steps it has already taken to comply with federal civil rights laws.
 "Protections for academic freedom and civil rights are expressly affirmed in the agreement. It makes clear that the federal government will not dictate the content of academic speech or curricula at Carolina," the university said.
 As for admissions, the Justice Department said UNC will adopt a "color-blind" admission system, which they said includes:
 Refraining from using race, analyzing racial data or altering its admission process to change the racial composition of its student body. 
 Disfavoring applicants who decline to identify their race. 
 Not use race in selecting admissions personel and may not partner with "bridge" or "pipeline" programs that consider any protected characteristic. 
 The settlement also says UNC would hire a "Merit & Civil Rights administrator" within the next 30 days. The administrator would be responsible for implementing the settlement agreement, as well as receiving quarterly reports on antisemitism and racial discrimination complaints they received.
 The settlement is in effect through the end of 2028.
